item.title: Stock earnings pick of the week: Can Applied Materials spot cracks in the AI spending boom?
item.description:
Spend, spend, spend. That's been the name of the game in the AI boom over the past two years. But really, just how much longer can the industry keep throwing money at bigger and better chips before someone starts asking whether the returns are worth it? Well, Applied Materials might give us a few clues this week.

The semiconductor equipment giant reports earnings on Thursday this week. And just like the rest of the other tech earnings these days, I would be less interested in whether it can beat Wall Street's estimates. Instead, I'd focus much more on what the company has to say about the next round of spending.

I mean you would think that if the AI investment frenzy is beginning to lose steam, then the companies supplying the tools to build those chips might be among the first to notice.

Everyone loves a gold rush, especially the folks selling the shovels. And in the AI boom, Applied Materials is very much in the business of selling those shovels.

Wall Street is expecting revenue of $10.30 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $4.06, compared with $6.80 billion and $2.17 respectively a year ago. That's quite a big leap and one that speaks to the relentless spending on advanced chips and manufacturing capacity.

For some context, Applied Materials delivered record revenue of $9.12 billion in the previous quarter with non-GAAP earnings per share of $3.50. At the time, the management laid out an ambitious longer-term outlook, expecting wafer fabrication equipment spending to grow faster through 2030 than over the past decade. However, we have seen how things can quickly change in the past quarter with other big tech firms. So, this is where things might get a little tricky.

The bottom line now is that strong AI demand doesn't automatically guarantee that the current pace of capital expenditure is sustainable.

Chipmakers are pouring money into manufacturing, high-bandwidth memory and advanced packaging. And Applied Materials sits right in the middle of that spending cycle, supplying the equipment needed to make these growingly more complex chips.

As such, I'll be watching whether the management continues to see accelerating demand from leading-edge foundry and DRAM customers. Besides that, any indication that orders or capacity expansion plans are being pushed further into 2027 will also be a key signal to watch this week.

But perhaps most importantly is the question of will customers keep spending at this pace if the returns on AI infrastructure investment take longer to materialise?

A more confident outlook could lend support to semiconductor equipment names and the wider AI trade in broader markets. However, any suggestion of slowing investment commitments could revive concerns over how much optimism is already priced into tech stocks.

As has been the case in the past month, markets have come to terms that the AI boom has already delivered plenty of impressive numbers. What they need now is more concrete evidence that the spending can keep going without eventually running ahead of the returns.

And that's the same narrative in play when looking at Applied Materials' earnings this week.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: What is the distribution of forecasts for the US CPI?
item.description:
The ranges of estimates are important in terms of market reaction because when the actual data deviates from the expectations, it creates a surprise effect. Another important input in market's reaction is the distribution of forecasts.

In fact, although we can have a range of estimates, most forecasts might be clustered on the upper bound of the range, so even if the data comes out inside the range of estimates but on the lower bound of the range, it can still create a surprise effect.

CPI M/M

  • 0.5% (1%)
  • 0.4% (6%)
  • 0.3% (64%) - consensus
  • 0.2% (28%)
  • 0.1% (1%) 

Core CPI M/M

  • 0.3% (31%)
  • 0.2% (66%) - consensus
  • 0.1% (3%)

We won't get the Y/Y figures today because of the government shutdown last year. The focus will be on the Core CPI M/M measure where we can see that the expectations are skewed to the upside. 

Fed's Waller delivered some very hawkish comments today where he said that he would support a quarter-point rate hike in December even if October's CPI improves relative to September. Therefore, a soft report is not going to change much.

What traders will be looking at is if the Core CPI M/M comes in at 0.3% or higher as Waller said that he would vote for a larger 0.5% hike in such a case. He's a very influential Fed governor and has been a leading indicator for Fed policy since 2021, so his views are always important for the market.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Waller says a half-point rate hike in December may be needed if Core CPI comes in hot
item.description:
• Half-point Fed rate hike may be needed in December, if October Core CPI inflation comes in around 0.3% or higher
  • Would support quarter-point rate hike in December even if October CPI improves vs September
  • US inflation is too high, September's inflation data was bad
  • Was willing to wait on policy tightening in October; what matters is that promised hikes are delivered in a reasonable period of time
  • Particularly concerned about the breadth of price increases
  • Suspect GDP growth is backing off in current quarter, but output will continue to grow at solid pace
  • Fed staff analyses suggest more producer price increases ahead, and potential for energy price shock to be more persistent
  • Labor market solid, supply and demand roughly in balance, employment close to Fed's goal
  • Unclear if labour market is as healthy as the unemployment rate suggests; dynamism and productivity growth questions need more research

These are very hawkish remarks from Fed's governor Waller as he's suggesting that a rate hike in December would be warranted regardless of today's inflation data. The only thing that the data would change for him is the magnitude of the increase as a Core CPI M/M at 0.3% or higher would lead him to vote for a larger 0.5% hike. 

Waller stressed that US inflation remains too high and described September's inflation report as disappointing. He had been willing to wait on further policy tightening at the October meeting, but emphasised that what matters now is delivering the promised rate hikes within a reasonable period of time. He also highlighted concerns about the breadth of price increases, suggesting that inflationary pressures remain more widespread than he would like.

He acknowledged that GDP growth may be slowing in the current quarter, although he still expects output to expand at a solid pace. He noted that Fed staff analyses point to further producer price increases ahead and warned that the energy price shock could prove more persistent than initially expected.

Regarding the labour market, Waller described conditions as broadly solid, with supply and demand roughly in balance and employment close to Fed's objectives. However, he cautioned that the unemployment rate alone may not fully capture the health of the labour market, pointing to questions surrounding labour market dynamism and productivity growth that require further analysis.

Keep in mind that Waller is a very influential governor and has been a leading indicator for Fed's policy since 2021. He's been willing to give disinflation a chance back in September but has now drastically changed his mind. The probabilities for a December hike jumped to 99% following Waller's comments (the 1% is for a 0.5% hike).

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold holds near recent highs as markets await US CPI and Iran breakthrough
item.description:
Gold edged higher yesterday but couldn’t extend the gains above the recent highs as markets continue to wait for concrete US-Iran developments and the US CPI data.  

On the US-Iran front, we got some positive headlines yesterday that led to an improvement in risk sentiment as hopes for a deal strengthened again.

It was reported that meetings between Trump, Vance and the Qatari PM were positive, and they discussed ways to progress talks with Iran.

Trump said after talks with the Qatari PM that Qatar would rather see a peaceful solution with Iran, but the US is ready for strikes if necessary.

Moreover, it was reported that the US has allowed a small uranium enrichment inside Iran, which Tehran agreed to, and preliminary agreement on reducing uranium enrichment is likely.

On the US CPI side, the data today could seal a rate hike for the December FOMC meeting, with traders already pricing in an 84% probability.

If we get a hot report, we could see a downward spike in gold, but I would expect the losses to be faded. This is because rate hikes at this point should put even more downward pressure on the stock market and long-term Treasury yields amid growth concerns, barring an end to the Iran war. Soft data, on the other hand, should trigger an immediate rally on a dovish repricing.

Keep in mind that in the current context, if Trump decides to escalate the war, inflation expectations would rise alongside weakening growth outlook, creating a stagflationary environment. This should be bullish for gold. At the same time, if we get a de-escalation, we could see a dovish repricing on easing inflation concerns, which should also support gold in the short-term.

 

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that gold(CFD contract) is still consolidating above the broken trendline. The buyers will likely continue to pile in around these levels, with a defined risk below the trendline, to keep targeting new highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will need to see the price breaking below the major upward trendline to open the door for new lows.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we have a minor support zone around the 4,040 level. If we get another pullback, we can expect the buyers to step in around the support, with a defined risk below the minor upward trendline, to keep targeting the 4,500 level. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break below the upward trendline to extend the pullback into the major trendline next.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we have another minor upward trendline that could act as support. We can expect the buyers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk below it, to keep targeting the 4,500 level. The sellers, on the other hand, look for a break lower to extend the pullback into the 4,040 support next. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

Todaywe have the US CPI report. Tomorrow, we get the latest US Jobless Claims figures. On Friday, we conclude the week with the US PPI data.

item.title: European stock market open: Stocks rally across the board as market optimism grows
item.description:
Well, well, well. European stocks are certainly in a good mood today. And why not? Oil prices are retreating amid hopes of easing US-Iran tensions as investors are finding reasons to put last week's jitters behind them. The positive momentum from yesterday is carrying over into Tuesday trading, with major indices posting strong gains across the board.

  • Eurostoxx +1.1%
  • Germany DAX +1.2%
  • France CAC 40 +1.2%
  • UK FTSE +0.7%
  • Spain IBEX +1.2%
  • Italy FTSE MIB +1.3%

It's a sea of green for European equities with gains of over 1% across most major indices. Lower oil prices are offering some welcome relief to the inflation outlook, particularly for Europe given its exposure to imported energy costs. So, that is giving investors a reason to reassess the economic damage from the recent energy shock over the past few months.

That being said, I'd be careful about getting too carried away with the optimism. Falling oil prices may be taking some pressure off the inflation outlook but that doesn't necessarily mean the broader problem is going away just yet.

And with the US CPI report coming up later today, we could get yet another reminder of just how much work central banks might still have ahead of them.

Headline inflation is expected to slow to 0.3% m/m in October, down from 0.6% in September. Meanwhile, core inflation is estimated to ease to 0.2% m/m - down from 0.3% previously. Markets are still pricing roughly an 84% probability of another Fed rate hike in December, so that leaves little room for an upside inflation surprise.

For European equities, I would argue that the bigger risk isn't necessarily the inflation numbers themselves. It is more about how US Treasury yields react afterwards. A hotter report could send yields higher, revive concerns over tighter financial conditions and take some shine off the rally in equities. On the flip side, softer inflation alongside falling oil prices could give buyers another reason to extend the recovery.

For now though, dip buyers are still holding the upper hand. But with the US CPI report still to come, there is every reason for markets to heed some caution.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Macro pulse: Wall Street's relief rally is looking good but what happens next?
item.description:
Wall Street is certainly enjoying itself again to start the new week. The S&P 500 surged by 2.3% yesterday, its best performance since April, as falling oil prices and hopes of a de-escalation in the US-Iran war gave investors a reason to pile back into stocks.

Fair enough. Cheaper oil prices help to take some pressure off inflation, which then eases the squeeze on corporate costs and household spending. So, that's good news for stocks especially after the brutal selloff last week.

But now, what happens when all that optimism is starting to get priced into markets? Let's think about if for a second. A potential end to the Middle East conflict removes one major source of uncertainty for equities. However, it doesn't necessarily give stocks a fresh catalyst to keep pushing higher endlessly.

As such, I would argue that there are three things worth watching to judge whether this latest rebound has any staying power.

The first one is that Treasury yields need to also play along.

10-year Treasury yields are hovering just below 4.90% and that's hardly an invitation for investors to throw caution to the wind. If oil prices keep falling but bond yields remain elevated, any real benefit to equity valuations could prove to be limited once the dust settles.

Adding to that, Washington's fiscal outlook isn't helping either. Persistent deficits and heavy borrowing requirements could continue to underping long-term yields especially, even as geopolitical risks fade.

Besides that, cheaper oil alone isn't going to change the Fed's thinking overnight. Markets are still pricing in roughly an 84% chance of a December rate hike, so there are still some hawkish undertones for traders to manage. The first test of which will come later today from the US CPI report.

The second thing is to see whether the equities rally can broaden beyond the usual suspects.

The rebound yesterday was definitely encouraging, with all 11 sectors of the finishing higher and the Russell 2000 gaining by 3.1%. The question now though is can that very momentum continue?

If small caps, industrials and consumer discretionary stocks keep participating, that would suggest investors are buying into a healthier economic outlook rather than simply chasing another technology rebound. As for a rally that is carried by fewer and fewer stocks? Well, that's a completely different story.

And lastly, earnings also need to pull their weight and justify the enthusiasm.

Now, the AI spending debate hasn't disappeared just because oil prices are falling. Investors still need a lot of convincing that the enormous capex commitments will eventually translate into sustainable profit growth. But if valuations keep rising faster than earnings expectations, we're only likely to see the market turn to become more vulnerable to another disappointment.

So, that is the broader picture that I'll be watching next even as geopolitical tensions start to ease from hereon.

A genuine de-escalation in the US-Iran war could certainly lay the groundwork for a sustained recovery. However, I'd also want to see falling bond yields, broader equity participation and stronger earnings expectations to reinforce that optimism.

Otherwise, we could end up with a case of market players already buying into the good news but haven't quite figured out what comes next. And that's when the easy part of the rally comes to an end.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Learn technical analysis without being a professor: This repeating pattern is super simple and super effective
item.description:
Gold futures: A breakout, a retest, and another move higher

You don't need to be a professor to learn technical analysis. This simple pattern on gold's 4-hour chart offers a valuable lesson about identifying the stronger side of the market, even if you use a completely different trading strategy.

My 4-hour gold chart from today, November 10, is super simple. No indicators, zero noise. And I can tell you that once you practice recognizing these patterns, they can become an extremely useful part of your trading analysis.

But let's clarify something first.

"Effective" does NOT mean you will always profit.

Patterns matter because they give you guidance about which side of the market is currently stronger. That can help you develop an edge, although no particular win rate is guaranteed. Experience, confirmation, execution and risk management all matter.

It also doesn't mean prices cannot change direction later, that other patterns don't matter, or that something unexpected won't happen five minutes from now and change the market entirely.

With that in mind, let's look at gold.

Gold's 4-hour chart: Three simple observations

Gold futures had been moving lower inside a channel, between two downward-sloping lines.

Some traders would look at this as a potential bullish continuation pattern, similar to a bull flag.

Now look at the three numbered points on the chart.

Point 1: The breakout

Gold moved above the upper line of the descending channel.

This is called a breakout.

It's the first indication that buyers may be becoming stronger and that the downward structure could be ending.

But a breakout doesn't automatically mean prices will continue rising. Sometimes they fail, and prices return inside the original channel.

That's why the next observation is important.

Point 2: The retest

After the breakout, gold moved lower and returned to the channel line it had previously crossed.

This is called a retest, and it happens quite often in financial markets.

The idea is simple. An area that previously acted as resistance, making it difficult for prices to move higher, may later become support, where buyers are willing to step in.

In this case, gold returned to the breakout area around $4,050-$4,070 and then moved higher again.

That's another positive sign for the bulls.

Point 3: The move higher continues

After the retest, gold started moving higher again.

At the time of the chart, gold futures were trading near $4,130.

The next area I'm watching is around $4,150-$4,160.

If gold breaks above this area and can hold there, that would provide further evidence that buyers remain in control.

On the other hand, a move back inside the old descending channel would weaken the bullish interpretation.

So, for now, the bulls appear stronger than the bears on this timeframe. That doesn't mean I know what gold will do next. It means the available price structure favors one side over the other.

A different way to look at bull flags and bear flags

Traditionally, technical analysts identify a bull flag as a strong upward move (the pole), followed by downward-sloping consolidation and a potential breakout higher. A classic bear flag is the opposite.

But many years ago, I learned an interesting approach from a market expert who already had 15 years of experience.

Look at almost every ascending channel as a potential bear flag, and almost every descending channel as a potential bull flag.

That's something I still do today.

The keyword is potential.

A descending channel becomes more interesting to bulls when price breaks above it. An ascending channel becomes more interesting to bears when price breaks below it.

But here's where it gets particularly interesting.

If an ascending channel breaks upwards instead, that's an especially bullish development. And if a descending channel breaks downwards, that's an especially bearish development.

Why? Because instead of reversing the previous direction of the channel, price demonstrates enough strength or weakness to break out in that same direction.

These aren't necessarily textbook flags, and a breakout alone doesn't guarantee a sustained move. But observing whether price breaks out, fails, or successfully retests a channel can provide extremely useful information.

Why learn these patterns if you already have a trading strategy?

You don't have to trade bull flags or draw trendlines as part of your own strategy.

Maybe you prefer moving averages, VWAP, Fibonacci levels, order flow or something completely different.

That's fine.

But recognizing common price patterns gives you another perspective on what the market is doing.

For example, suppose your trading strategy gives you a signal to buy.

If the larger chart also shows a successful bullish breakout, a retest and a continuation higher, you have additional evidence supporting that direction.

Now imagine the opposite.

Your strategy tells you to sell, but the larger chart shows buyers repeatedly defending support and pushing prices higher.

Wouldn't that be useful information to consider before entering a short position?

It doesn't necessarily mean your strategy is wrong. It means you have another piece of evidence to evaluate.

And that's the main lesson I want to share.

You don't need to change your trading strategy to benefit from understanding other methods.

Learn to recognize patterns. Watch what happens when they break out, when they fail and when prices return to test important areas.

Over time, this can help you better understand which side of the market has the advantage, identify potential opportunities and recognize when the evidence is changing.

For gold right now, the 4-hour chart tells a fairly simple story: breakout, retest, continuation. Buyers have shown greater strength.

Could that change? Absolutely.

But until the price action tells us otherwise, there's no reason to ignore what the chart is showing us.

Patterns matter. And sometimes, keeping things simple is the best place to start.

--------------------------------

According to the latest technical breakdown at investingLive.com, gold's 4-hour chart continues to flash a simple yet highly effective repeating pattern that active traders should be watching closely.

The current structure clearly shows that bulls have the upper hand over bears, keeping gold's price action skewed to the upside amid a favorable macro backdrop.

While market conditions can always shift, betting against this momentum right now is a losing proposition, as pattern recognition remains critical.

This bullish resilience is especially notable given the broader headwinds across the commodities space, standing firm even as major institutions revise their broader outlook, such as the recent update where Goldman Sachs cut its 2026 and 2027 gold targets due to a hawkish Fed.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US CPI preview: Wall Street sees cooler inflation but the Fed may not blink
item.description:
Perhaps one of the more intriguing prospects heading into the US CPI report today is what if inflation cools and the Fed simply decides to shrug it off? Well, that may very well happen.

Wall Street is expecting a softer inflation reading for October but I wouldn't be so quick to assume that it will be enough to change the Fed's thinking ahead of the December meeting. The consensus estimate is for headline inflation to rise by 0.3% m/m in October, down from 0.6% in September. Meanwhile, core inflation is expected to ease to 0.2% m/m - down from 0.3% in the month before.

Morgan Stanley and Bank of America are both leaning towards an even softer headline reading of 0.2%. The former sees core inflation slowing to just 0.19%, with shelter, hotel prices, airfares and education costs normalising after September's unusually strong readings. But even so, the latter isn't quite buying the idea that cooler inflation will be enough to derail another Fed rate hike in December.

BofA argues that a 0.2% core reading would still effectively lock in a December move, with "only an indisputably soft 0.1% reading could affect the calculus".

And markets are also already leaning heavily in that direction. Fed funds futures are pricing in roughly an 84% probability of a 25 bps rate hike for December, suggesting that traders are hardly expecting today's inflation report to throw the Fed off course.

If anything else, that also means there is arguably more room for disappointment if the data surprises to the downside; as compared to potential for any further excitement from a reading that merely reinforces existing expectations.

So, what can we expect from the dollar in this case? MUFG is one to warn that the greenback is already running ahead of short-term yield spreads, suggesting that it may take a hawkish inflation surprise to sustain its recent strength.

In other words, even an inflation report that keeps the Fed on track to hike rates might not necessarily be enough to give dollar bulls another reason to celebrate. As such, the firm is targeting EUR/USD to be at 1.12 and USD/JPY at 155 by year-end.

As a reminder, just be wary that there's also a statistical wrinkle to today's release. The BLS will not publish the usual annual inflation comparisons because of missing October 2025 data during last year's government shutdown. So, that leaves the monthly readings carrying even more weight.

And for the bigger picture, the real question today isn't just whether inflation pressures are showing signs of cooling. It's whether they are seen cooling enough to force the Fed and markets to rethink December.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Heads up: Any US CPI fireworks may fizzle out as Veterans Day holiday looms
item.description:
The market is ready for some late night fireworks from the US CPI report later today but what happens if half the people decide not to show up for the after party to follow? That's something worth keeping in mind as we head towards tomorrow.

Wednesday will be a partial US market holiday in observance of Veterans Day and the timing is made rather awkward with the CPI report due later today.

The US bond market will be closed tomorrow but the NYSE and Nasdaq will remain open for trading as usual. However, don't mistake that for being business as usual on Wall Street.

Big banks and major fixed-income desks will be out of action. So if anything, I would expect thinner participation and potentially less conviction behind any sudden market moves. That especially after traders get their hands on the latest US inflation numbers today.

It would be less complicated if the inflation data only moves the stock market. However, Treasury yields are often at the heart of the reaction and that will in turn feed into the dollar, equities, and broader risk sentiment.

As such, when you take the bond market out of the equation tomorrow then suddenly we're missing one of the biggest drivers of that price discovery and gauge of market sentiment.

So, what does this mean for traders exactly?

If the US CPI report today delivers a major surprise, we could see the initial reaction carry through into tomorrow. But without meaningful Treasury market participation, the follow-through might struggle to find much traction.

There's another catch to all of this though. Thinner liquidity conditions don't necessarily mean smaller market moves. Such a situation can also exaggerate price swings, particularly if a large order hits when there aren't enough buyers or sellers on the other side.

As such, don't be too surprised if we get some choppy, directionless trading or even sudden moves that don't quite have the conviction to stick.

If anything, the bigger test will come on Thursday when the bond market returns and traders can properly reassess the inflation story with fuller participation. So until then, I'd be wary of reading too much into tomorrow's price action as markets might not be describing the full story. Sometimes, it can simply just be a case of having fewer people in the room.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: US CPI takes centre stage as markets look to steady the ship after the midterm selloff
item.description:
So, what'd I miss?

It's been quite a buzzing start to the week but today, it seems that markets might settle for doing nothing - at least in European morning trade. The US inflation data is looming later and I suspect European traders might be more than happy to sit on their hands until then.

US CPI day means that the inflation numbers will be the main event for markets. As such, I wouldn't expect much excitement in the hours to follow as traders keep their powder dry ahead of the release; that unless we get some surprise headlines during the session.

The October report is expected to show headline inflation rising by 0.3% m/m, easing from 0.6% in September. Meanwhile, core inflation is estimated to slow to 0.2% m/m, down from 0.3% previously.

Just be wary though that there is an important caveat to the release this time around. The BLS will not be publishing the usual annual comparisons for today's report, owing to missing October 2025 data during the government shutdown last year. As such, that puts even more emphasis on the monthly readings.

The bigger question later today is whether the numbers will give markets another reason to feel better about themselves, especially after tech shares have rebounded quite well since the selloff last week.

The Nasdaq gained another 2.7% yesterday while the S&P 500 climbed by 2.3% as risk appetite recovered alongside a sharp decline in oil prices. Even though tech shares have found their footing again, concerns surrounding AI spending and potential regulatory hurdles haven't exactly disappeared.

As such, today's inflation report might be one to help tip the balance of scales in that regard.

A softer report could offer some welcome relief for equities, particularly if it helps temper expectations for another Fed rate hike in December. Meanwhile, a hotter print risks throwing another spanner in the works considering that the recent recovery is still finding its legs. Hotter inflation could spark Treasury yields to nudge higher again and weigh on the already expensive tech valuations further.

But for now, I suspect traders will be reluctant to chase the rebound too aggressively before getting a clearer inflation signal.

In any case, Europe will be facing a quieter session in the day ahead with the real fireworks reserved for the US data later today.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

  • UK retail sales rise 1.5%, best since June, but fuel costs and Budget caution weigh

  • Asset managers stay constructive on stocks after AI rout, urge investors to diversify
  • Trump says renewed Iran strikes ‘quite unlikely’ as Gulf allies back blockade status quo
  • WSJ: Anthropic targets Nasdaq debut next week under ticker ANT despite tech selloff

Summary:

  • The KOSPI rose about 3.7% and the Nikkei about 2.4% as AI and chip stocks extended their rebound, though both came off session highs
  • Brent fell toward $92 and WTI to around $86 after Trump said renewed strikes on Iran look unlikely; Tehran demanded the US accept its seven conditions
  • China’s October exports rose 35.2% and imports 41.6%, pushing the year-to-date trade surplus past $1 trillion
  • The BoJ’s Summary of Opinions leaned hawkish, while Japan’s household spending slumped 6.8%
  • Australian business conditions and consumer sentiment both hit multi-year lows; Canberra will create an AI regulator
  • Anthropic retracted IPO pricing details it had sent to bankers; US CPI is due at 13:30 GMT

Equities

Asian stocks extended their rebound from Friday’s tech-led rout on Tuesday, with AI and chip shares again leading the way, though gains eased from the session’s highs as the day wore on.

South Korea’s KOSPI rose about 3.7% to around 5,200 by early afternoon, having traded as high as 5,300 earlier. Samsung Electronics gained more than 4% and SK Hynix nearly 6%. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was up about 2.4% near 60,160, after touching almost 60,780, while the broader Topix gained about 1.7%. SoftBank Group, Tokyo Electron and memory maker Kioxia were among the standout gainers in Tokyo.

The rally held up despite a 4.2% overnight fall in Nvidia amid controversy surrounding its chief executive, which strategists in Tokyo described as a company-specific issue. A strategist also noted investors’ reluctance to push the Nikkei above 61,000. Elsewhere, gains were slim, with Hong Kong’s Hang Seng up about 0.4% and Shanghai barely changed. US Nasdaq 100 futures slipped about 0.4%.

Oil and geopolitics

Oil prices eased as signals from Washington pointed away from renewed conflict with Iran. Brent fell about 0.8% to near $92 a barrel and WTI dropped about 1% to around $86.

US President Donald Trump said renewed military action against Iran now looks quite unlikely after a call with Qatar’s prime minister. He added that Gulf states prefer to keep the US naval blockade in place, alongside the new Iron Gate effort targeting Iran’s land routes. Tehran pushed back. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, dismissed reports of talks as fake news and told Washington to accept Iran’s seven conditions, including lifting the blockade, before any negotiations.

China’s CITIC Securities described the conflict as bounded: escalation is restrained by Congress and US public opinion, while a deal is blocked by demands neither US party will accept. That leaves a lower risk premium on crude, but a supply floor while Hormuz traffic remains disrupted.

China

China’s October exports rose 35.2% from a year earlier, beating forecasts as AI hardware demand held up, while imports surged 41.6%. The monthly surplus narrowed to about $105 billion, but the January-October total passed $1 trillion for a second straight year, a month earlier than in 2025. Crude imports hit their highest volume since March as buyers replaced disrupted Middle East supply.

The surplus is likely to sharpen trade frictions. China has extended its trade truce with the US by two months, and Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at next week’s APEC summit in Shenzhen. Separately, FedEx said it is adding four weekly China-US freighter flights aimed at AI infrastructure and semiconductor cargo.

Japan

The Bank of Japan’s Summary of Opinions from its October meeting showed the debate has moved from whether to raise rates to how quickly. Several members urged a faster move to neutral, and one put the neutral rate considerably above 1%. More cautious members pointed to weak consumption, a concern underlined by September household spending, which fell 6.8% from a year earlier against expectations for a 3.1% decline. Markets continue to expect a hike to 1.5% in December. The yen was little changed near 158 per dollar.

Australia

Domestic data pointed to an economy under strain. NAB’s business conditions index fell to -2, its lowest since August 2020, and the Westpac-Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index dropped to a four-year low of 78.2 after the Reserve Bank of Australia’s fifth hike of the year to 4.85%. Westpac expects the RBA to pause in December. The government also said it will create an AI regulator and require AI companies to report breaches, after an OpenAI agent accessed a Medicare data portal. The Australian dollar edged lower to around 0.692.

AI and corporate

Anthropic sent bankers IPO terms showing about 867 million shares at $70 to $80 each, then retracted the pricing details as inaccurate and said it would update its filing. Goldman Sachs expects AI-related investment grade financing to reach around $1.5 trillion over three years, warning that heavy supply is a headwind for credit.

Ahead

US October CPI is due at 13:30 GMT (08:30 US Eastern). Economists expect a 0.3% monthly rise in headline prices and 0.2% in core. No official annual rate will be published, because last year’s government shutdown left a gap in the October 2025 data.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China trade recap: surplus tops $1 trillion as AI boom powers exports, tensions loom
item.description:
Strong AI-led exports support Asian tech and supply-chain stocks, adding to today’s regional rebound. The bigger issue is political. A surplus above $1 trillion makes new trade barriers more likely, from the EU in particular, and puts trade at the centre of next week’s Xi-Trump meeting. The rebound in China’s crude imports to the highest since March, as buyers replace disrupted Middle East supply, is a supportive signal for oil demand even as prices ease on Iran de-escalation hopes. The import surge is a modest positive for commodity exporters and the Australian dollar, though weak Chinese consumer demand limits how far that read can be pushed.

---

China’s AI-fuelled export machine has pushed the trade surplus past $1 trillion again, which is great for factories and awkward for diplomacy.

Summary:

  • China’s October exports rose 35.2% year on year, beating the 33.5% forecast; imports jumped 41.6% against 32% expected
  • The January-October surplus reached about $1.04 trillion, topping $1 trillion for a second year and a month earlier than in 2025
  • Crude imports fell 13.3% from a year earlier but hit their highest volume since March, as buyers replaced Middle East supply disrupted by the Iran war
  • Demand at home remains weak, with domestic car sales down for a 12th month while car exports grew
  • Trade friction is in focus: the EU wants more curbs, and Xi and Trump are expected to meet at next week’s APEC summit
  • Analysts expect exports to accelerate in the fourth quarter before slowing from early 2027

China’s trade surplus topped $1 trillion in the first 10 months of the year as the global race to build AI infrastructure powered exports of high-tech goods, offsetting weak demand at home and setting up fresh friction with trading partners. Here is a recap of Tuesday’s data and what it means.

Exports rose 35.2% in October from a year earlier in US dollar terms, customs data showed. That was ahead of forecasts for a 33.5% gain and only a touch slower than September’s 36.3%. Imports jumped 41.6%, far above the 32% expected. The import surge narrowed the monthly surplus to about $105 billion, but it still lifted the January-October total to about $1.04 trillion. That is the second straight year above $1 trillion, and the milestone came a month earlier than in 2025.

The surplus with the US eased slightly to about $33 billion from $34 billion in September. Crude oil imports fell 13.3% from a year earlier, although shipments reached their highest level since March as buyers sought supplies after the war on Iran disrupted Middle East flows.

AI demand remains the engine. Much of this year’s export strength has come from hardware for data centres, and FedEx this week added freighter capacity between China and the US aimed squarely at AI infrastructure and semiconductors. Analysts expect exports to accelerate further in the fourth quarter before slowing from early 2027, with the outlook hinging on how long the AI boom lasts.

At home, the picture is weaker. Consumers remain reluctant to spend amid a prolonged property downturn, and domestic vehicle sales fell for a 12th straight month even as car exports grew. That reliance on overseas demand leaves China more exposed to any global slowdown. Chinese stocks have also struggled, prompting Beijing to step up market support after the CSI 300 suffered its worst month in more than a decade in October. Mainland and Hong Kong shares edged higher on Tuesday, while regional tech stocks rallied more strongly.

Trade politics will now take centre stage. China has extended its trade truce with Washington by two months, and Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at next week’s APEC summit in Shenzhen, their third meeting this year. In Europe, leaders have called for more curbs on Chinese goods. Analysts warn the risk of new tariffs will stay elevated into 2027 as Chinese manufacturers keep expanding overseas.  

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia to mandate AI breach reporting, set up regulator after OpenAI agent breach
item.description:
For markets, the significance is less Australia itself than the precedent. Mandatory incident reporting and an AI safety regulator with penalty powers offer a template other governments could adopt, adding to compliance costs for AI developers across jurisdictions. That reinforces the regulatory-risk theme that helped drive last week’s AI selloff after the US midterms, though the rebound in Asian tech today suggests investors aren’t treating each new rule as a threat to the build-out. Rules on autonomous agents, rather than on models alone, mark a widening of the regulatory net that companies relying on agent-based products will need to price in.

-

One AI agent wandering into a health data portal has given Australia its blueprint for AI regulation, and other governments are likely to be taking notes.

Summary:

  • Australia will require AI companies to report misaligned behaviour and cyber incidents, and will consider criminal law reform for serious misconduct
  • A new AI regulator will oversee security controls, identify serious risks, evaluate models independently and impose significant penalties
  • The moves follow an OpenAI agent’s unauthorised access to a Medicare statistics portal; OpenAI says it was unintentional and that no patient records were accessed
  • OpenAI and Anthropic told parliament they would welcome mandatory breach reporting
  • The step adds to tightening AI oversight globally, from the EU to the US after the midterms

Australia will require artificial intelligence companies to report breaches and will create a dedicated AI regulator, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday, after an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to a government health data portal. The move puts Australia among the more assertive governments on AI oversight, at a time when regulatory risk has become a live issue for investors worldwide.

The government said in September that an OpenAI agent had broken into the medical statistics portal of Medicare, the country’s universal health insurance scheme, while researching public medical spending. A rapid review followed, and Albanese said the government had accepted all of its recommendations. These include mandatory reporting by AI companies of misaligned behaviour or cyber incidents, and consideration of criminal law reform for cases of serious misconduct.

The new regulator would oversee security controls across the development and deployment of AI systems, identify serious risks and carry out independent evaluations of models, with powers to impose significant penalties. The measures will form part of AI legislation the government plans to introduce next year.

OpenAI has said it learned of the breach in August, that the incident was unintentional, and that its review found no evidence patient records were accessed. Both OpenAI and rival Anthropic told the Australian parliament last month that they would welcome laws requiring them to report breaches by their AI agents, acknowledging that disclosure is currently at their discretion.

The episode adds to friction between Canberra and US technology companies. Australia has already refused the two firms exemptions from copyright law for model training, requiring them to negotiate licences with local rights holders.

The broader significance lies in the direction of travel. AI agents that act autonomously online are moving from demonstration to deployment, and this case shows how quickly a single incident can turn into binding rules. Australia’s approach echoes the European Union’s phased rollout of its AI Act. It also lands as investors reassess regulatory risk in the United States, where Democratic gains in last week’s midterm elections raised expectations of tougher scrutiny of AI and data centres, a concern that helped drive last week’s sharp selloff in AI stocks.

For AI developers, the cost of compliance is rising across jurisdictions just as the sector seeks vast sums of capital, including through Anthropic’s planned share sale. Other governments are likely to study mandatory incident reporting closely as a template.

---

Australian prime minister Albanese

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nikkei, KOSPI extend rebound as AI and chip stocks surge, recouping Friday’s rout
item.description:
The rebound suggests investors see last week’s AI selloff as a positioning shakeout rather than a turn in the cycle. That fits the wealth managers’ view this morning and the strong AI-led export numbers from China. Holding up despite Nvidia’s fall points to the market treating that issue as company-specific for now. Lower oil prices are a second tailwind, especially for energy importers such as Korea and Japan, though Brent near $92 keeps the energy cost burden high. The Nikkei’s hesitation below 61,000 suggests the rebound may need fresh catalysts, with US CPI later today the next test for tech sentiment.

---

Asia’s AI trade has shaken off Friday’s scare and even Nvidia’s stumble, but Tokyo’s reluctance above 61,000 shows the conviction isn’t fully back.

Summary:

  • The Nikkei rose about 2.7% near 60,400 and the Topix about 2.2%, recouping most of Friday’s near-6% drop over two sessions
  • The KOSPI jumped more than 4% to around 5,240, led by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix
  • SoftBank surged over 14%, with Advantest, Tokyo Electron and Kioxia also sharply higher
  • The gains came despite Nvidia’s 4.2% overnight fall, which strategists see as stock-specific
  • Lower oil prices, on hopes for an end to the US-Iran war, lifted Korean airlines and supported sentiment

Japanese and South Korean stocks extended their rebound on Tuesday as AI-related shares climbed again, recovering much of the ground lost in Friday’s tech-led selloff.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 was up around 2.7% near 60,400 in early afternoon trade, while the broader Topix gained about 2.2%. In Seoul, the KOSPI jumped more than 4% to around 5,240, with the tech-heavy KOSDAQ up nearly 4%.

Chip and AI names led the way. In Tokyo, SoftBank Group surged more than 14%, chip equipment makers Advantest and Tokyo Electron gained around 5% to 6%, and memory maker Kioxia jumped more than 7%. Kioxia was a key driver of the Nikkei’s run to a record high in June but has since been hit by weaker sentiment toward AI shares. In Seoul, Samsung Electronics rose about 5% and SK Hynix around 6%.

The gains came despite a 4.2% fall in Nvidia overnight amid controversy surrounding its chief executive, Jensen Huang. A Tokyo-based strategist said the market so far sees the issue as specific to Nvidia rather than a problem for the wider industry.

The Nikkei had fallen nearly 6% on Friday on concerns that Democratic gains in the US midterm elections could slow AI investment. Two sessions of strong gains have now recouped most of those losses, though the same strategist said investors were reluctant to push the index above 61,000.

Lower oil prices added support, particularly in Seoul. Hopes for an end to the US-Iran war pulled crude lower and eased inflation worries, helping Wall Street close higher overnight. Korean Air and Asiana Airlines each rallied more than 11%. Brent crude was trading around $92 a barrel and US WTI near $86, both modestly lower on the day.

Elsewhere in the region, gains were more modest. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng was up about 0.5% and Shanghai around 0.3%. In Tokyo, Toyota was the biggest drag on the Topix. The yen was little changed around 158 per dollar after the Bank of Japan’s Summary of Opinions earlier in the session. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China October exports beat forecasts, imports surge 41.6% as trade surplus narrows
item.description:
Stronger-than-expected exports suggest physical demand for AI hardware held up through October, offering some support to Asian tech and supply-chain stocks after last week’s selloff. The import surprise is the more notable signal. If it reflects firmer domestic demand rather than just higher commodity prices, it would be a positive for commodity exporters and the Australian dollar, which also trades as a China proxy. If higher oil prices drove much of the gain, it points to the energy shock lifting China’s import bill. A narrower surplus may slightly ease trade frictions ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting, though the year-to-date surplus remains very large.

-

Earlier:

  • FedEx adds four weekly China-US freighter flights as AI hardware demand keeps cargo busy

-

China’s trade engine is running hot in both directions, with AI hardware still flying out and a surprise surge in imports eating into the surplus.

Summary:

  • China’s October exports rose 35.2% year on year in dollar terms, beating the 33.5% forecast but slightly slower than September’s 36.3%
  • Imports jumped 41.6%, far above the 32% expected and up from 31% in September
  • The trade surplus narrowed to about $105 billion, short of the roughly $126 billion forecast and down from about $134 billion
  • AI-related hardware has been the main driver of China’s export boom this year
  • Import drivers are unclear pending the detailed data; higher commodity prices may be a factor

China’s exports grew faster than expected in October and imports surged well beyond forecasts, sharply narrowing the monthly trade surplus as trade flows stayed exceptionally strong.

Exports rose 35.2% from a year earlier in US dollar terms, ahead of the 33.5% median forecast in a Reuters poll, though slightly slower than September’s 36.3% gain. Imports jumped 41.6%, far above expectations for a 32% rise and accelerating from 31% the previous month.

The stronger import bill cut the trade surplus to about $105 billion, well short of the roughly $126 billion forecast and down from about $134 billion in September.

The export figures add to evidence that the global race to build AI infrastructure is still driving demand for Chinese-made hardware. Economists say shipments of components such as printed circuit boards, memory chips and optical transceivers have powered the surge in outbound trade this year. The October data suggest that momentum held up even as US AI stocks sold off on concerns over the pace of the data centre build-out. Some analysts had warned that a drop in new export orders in factory surveys could signal a softer tech cycle, but there is little sign of that in the headline numbers so far.

The import surge is harder to read without a detailed breakdown. Higher prices for crude oil and other commodities would lift the value of China’s purchases, and inbound shipments of chips and other components for assembly would also add to the total. The full customs data, due later, should show how much of the rise reflects prices rather than volumes.

The figures arrive at a sensitive moment for Beijing. Chinese stocks have been under heavy pressure, prompting authorities to step up support measures, and trade is expected to feature when US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen later this month. China’s large and persistent trade surplus has also risked antagonising trading partners, and a narrower monthly gap may ease some of that pressure at the margin. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: FedEx adds four weekly China-US freighter flights as AI hardware demand keeps cargo busy
item.description:
The move is a modest but concrete signal that physical demand for AI hardware from Asia remains firm. That contrasts with last week’s equity-market doubts about the pace of the US data centre build-out. If today’s China trade data confirms strong AI-related exports, it would support Asian semiconductor and hardware supply-chain stocks that sold off with US tech. Air cargo capacity aimed at AI components also points to ongoing volume for logistics and freight names. The main risks to that read are concrete state-level curbs on US data centres, or any trade friction around the expected Trump-Xi meeting.

-

Wall Street may be questioning the AI boom, but FedEx is betting there’s still plenty of AI hardware to fly out of China.

Summary:

  • FedEx is adding four weekly Boeing 777 freighter flights between China and the US
  • Three will fly from Shanghai via Osaka to Anchorage and Memphis, and one from Guangzhou to the same hubs
  • FedEx says the capacity targets advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, AI infrastructure and high-end e-commerce
  • The move comes ahead of China’s October trade data, with exports expected up about a third on AI hardware demand
  • Trade is likely to feature at an expected Trump-Xi meeting at the APEC summit in Shenzhen in mid-November

FedEx is adding four weekly freighter flights between China and the United States. It’s a small capacity move, but it offers a useful read on where demand in US-China trade is concentrated: AI hardware, semiconductors and advanced manufacturing.

The carrier said on November 9 that the new Boeing 777 freighter services will link Shanghai and Guangzhou with its US hubs. Three flights will depart Shanghai and stop in Osaka before continuing to Anchorage and Memphis, while the fourth will fly from Guangzhou to the same two hubs. FedEx said the extra capacity is aimed at advanced industrial manufacturing, semiconductor production, AI infrastructure and high-end e-commerce.

The sectors FedEx named are telling. Air freight is the transport of choice for high-value, time-sensitive goods such as chips, servers and networking equipment, and the global race to build AI infrastructure has sharply lifted the value of China’s outbound shipments this year. Economists expect China’s October trade data, due on Tuesday, to show exports up about a third from a year earlier in dollar terms, with demand for AI hardware a central driver.

The routing via Osaka also shows how tightly Asian supply chains for AI components are linked, with Japan a key source of semiconductor materials and production equipment.

The move comes against a mixed backdrop. US AI stocks sold off sharply last week on concerns that Democratic gains in the midterm elections could bring new limits on data centre construction, raising questions about the pace of the build-out. A logistics company adding capacity aimed squarely at AI infrastructure suggests that, on the ground, demand for the hardware is still flowing for now. Trade between the two countries is also likely to feature when US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet, as expected, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in mid-November.

For markets, the announcement is a modest but real-world signal that the AI supply chain from Asia to the US remains busy, even as investors debate how long the spending boom can last.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Anthropic retracts IPO pricing details sent to bankers, says figures were inaccurate
item.description:
The retraction adds uncertainty to a deal the market is treating as a benchmark for AI valuations after last week’s rout. Until a corrected filing appears, there is no confirmed range, share count or valuation for investors to anchor to. The errors look procedural rather than a change of plan, but the confusion comes just as investors are pressing for a lower valuation. That raises the chance that final terms land differently from the figures first circulated. AI-linked stocks may stay sensitive to headlines about the deal until the corrected filing is out.

--

Earlier, this is what is being retracted:

  • Anthropic lines up $26 billion from Nvidia, Google, others as IPO priced at $70 to $80

--

Anthropic’s IPO numbers went out and came straight back, so the most closely watched figure in AI, its valuation, is still unknown.

Summary:

  • Anthropic emailed bankers a filing showing plans to sell about 867 million shares at $70 to $80 each, then retracted the pricing details as inaccurate, according to emails seen by Reuters
  • The company said it would update the filing later and declined to comment
  • It is unclear whether a reported $26 billion private placement by Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC is affected
  • Investors have been pushing for a valuation below the roughly $1.5 trillion previously expected after last week’s AI selloff
  • Anthropic has been aiming to start trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ANT” as soon as Thursday or Friday next week

Anthropic sent bankers details of its planned initial public offering and then retracted them, saying the pricing information was inaccurate, according to emails seen by Reuters late on Monday.

The first email included a copy of a filing showing the Claude maker aimed to sell about 867 million shares at $70 to $80 each, terms that would have raised up to about $69 billion. A follow-up email said the pricing details were inaccurate and that Anthropic would update the filing later. The company declined to comment.

The retraction leaves the key numbers for one of the most closely watched listings of the year unconfirmed. Earlier reporting of the filing had also cited a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price by Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC. It is not yet clear whether that element is affected by the correction, or how far the final terms will differ from the figures first circulated.

The episode comes at a delicate point. Investors have been waiting for Anthropic’s valuation range, which the company was expected to set out in a filing early this week. The Wall Street Journal had reported that some major investors were pushing for a valuation below the roughly $1.5 trillion previously expected, after last week’s selloff in AI stocks wiped about $2.5 trillion off the Nasdaq Composite.

Anthropic has been aiming for its shares to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ANT” as soon as Thursday or Friday next week, according to the Journal. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are advising on the deal. There is no indication so far that the timetable has changed.

The corrected filing will now be the reference point for the share count, the price range and the implied valuation. Until it appears, the figures circulated on Monday should be treated as unconfirmed.

Intelligence ... yeah, right

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Anthropic lines up $26 billion from Nvidia, Google, others as IPO priced at $70 to $80
item.description:
Welll, before you read on, Anthropic has retracted!

  • Anthropic retracts IPO pricing details sent to bankers, says figures were inaccurate

---

The placement de-risks the deal at a fragile moment for AI stocks. Locking in $26 billion of demand before launch makes a weak debut less likely and could steady sentiment across AI names if pricing goes well. The supplier-as-investor structure may also feed concerns about circular financing in the AI sector, the same theme that has weighed on credit spreads and hyperscaler funding. For the wider market, the final price and implied valuation will set a benchmark for AI valuations after last week’s selloff. A deal priced at the top of the range would point to resilient appetite, while one at the bottom would suggest the reset has further to run.

----

Anthropic is going to market with its biggest suppliers as anchor buyers, a show of support that both steadies the deal and sharpens questions about who is funding the AI boom.

Summary:

  • Anthropic plans to sell about 867 million new shares at $70 to $80 each, raising up to about $69 billion, according to a filing seen by Reuters
  • Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC will invest a combined $26 billion through a private placement at the IPO price
  • The IPO and placement combined would raise roughly $87 billion to $95 billion; the IPO alone falls short of SpaceX’s roughly $75 billion record
  • The implied valuation was not disclosed
  • Shares are expected to start trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ANT” as soon as Thursday or Friday next week

Anthropic has lined up $26 billion from some of the biggest names in technology to buy shares alongside its initial public offering, setting terms for what could become the largest capital raise of any stock market debut.

The Claude maker plans to sell about 867 million new shares at $70 to $80 each, raising up to about $69 billion, according to a filing seen by Reuters. Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC will together invest a further $26 billion through a private placement at the IPO price.

Combined, the IPO and the placement would bring in roughly $87 billion to $95 billion. Even at the top of its range, the IPO alone falls short of the record of around $75 billion that SpaceX set in June, but the total including the placement would exceed it. Some early reports described the IPO as record-breaking, which holds only when the placement is included. The implied valuation has not been disclosed, because the total number of shares outstanding after the offering was not reported.

The list of anchor investors stands out. Every company named sells chips, memory or cloud capacity to AI developers, making them both suppliers to Anthropic and now shareholders. That ties the deal closely to the wider debate over how the AI build-out is being financed, and how much of it is funded by companies that also benefit from the spending.

The commitments come a week after a sharp selloff in AI stocks, when the Nasdaq Composite shed about $2.5 trillion in value following the US midterm elections. The Wall Street Journal had reported that some major investors were pushing Anthropic to accept a valuation below the roughly $1.5 trillion previously expected, and well below the $2 trillion floated months ago. Securing large committed buyers at the IPO price before launch reduces the risk of weak demand in a nervous market.

Anthropic is aiming for its shares to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ANT” as soon as Thursday or Friday next week, according to the Journal. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are advising on the deal. The final price, and the valuation it implies, will be the clearest test yet of public market appetite for AI after the recent rout.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australian consumer sentiment sinks to four-year low as rates and living costs bite
item.description:
Together with this morning’s NAB survey, the reading strengthens the case for an RBA pause in December and lowers the odds of a sixth hike. That leaves the Australian dollar with little support from rate expectations, at a time when it is already exposed to swings in AI-linked equities. Front-end Australian bond yields are the most sensitive to any shift toward pricing an earlier end to the tightening cycle. Above-target inflation and petrol prices near A$2.40 a litre keep the RBA from pivoting quickly. Lower oil prices would be the fastest route to relief for households.

-

Australian households are feeling as gloomy as they have only in genuine crises, and the RBA’s own rate hikes are a big part of why.

Summary:

  • The Westpac-Melbourne Institute Consumer Sentiment Index fell 2.7% to 78.2 in November, the lowest since late 2022
  • Readings this weak have otherwise only been seen during COVID, the global financial crisis and the recessions of the early 1980s and 1990s
  • Higher petrol prices, 4.3% inflation and a fifth RBA hike this year, to 4.85%, are driving the gloom; mortgage holders’ sentiment hit a record low
  • More than 70% of consumers expect mortgage rates to keep rising, and house price expectations turned negative
  • Westpac expects the RBA to pause in December and does not expect a hike in February

Australian consumer sentiment fell to a four-year low in November, as rising living costs and another interest rate hike pushed households deeper into pessimism, a Westpac and Melbourne Institute survey showed on Tuesday.

The Westpac-Melbourne Institute Consumer Sentiment Index dropped 2.7% to 78.2 from 80.4 in October, its weakest reading since late 2022. Westpac noted that, apart from that period, readings this low have only been seen in the economy’s darkest moments, including the onset of the COVID pandemic, the global financial crisis and the recessions of the early 1990s and 1980s.

Cost-of-living pressure remains the main driver. Over the past month petrol prices have pushed toward A$2.40 a litre and official inflation has reached 4.3%. The Reserve Bank of Australia has also raised the cash rate by another 25 basis points to 4.85%, an 18-year high. Westpac said any lift from the US midterm results had been swamped by inflation and rate worries. Sentiment among mortgage holders slumped to a record low on data back to 1994.

The November fall was led by a sharp deterioration in near-term expectations for the economy, which dropped to their weakest since August 2020. Households also turned negative on house prices for the first time since late 2022, and more than 70% of consumers expect mortgage rates to rise further over the coming year. Job-loss fears are edging higher, though Westpac described consumers as on edge rather than alarmed.

For the RBA, the survey adds to evidence that its five hikes this year are biting hard on rate-sensitive parts of the economy. Westpac expects the central bank to pause at its December 7-8 meeting to assess the impact of its tightening. It does not expect a hike in February either, though it cautioned that high inflation will continue to test the bank’s resolve.

The weak mood is a concern for retailers heading into Christmas. Even so, Westpac said gift-spending intentions have held up better than headline sentiment suggests, with mortgage holders the most likely to cut back.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: The view from China: CITIC sees Iran war risk ‘bounded’ as blockade outlasts US midterms
item.description:
CITIC’s “bounded” framing points oil toward a range rather than a trend. Limited escalation risk caps the upside for crude, while the absence of a negotiated exit keeps Iranian barrels off the market and Hormuz traffic restricted, which puts a floor under prices. That fits this week’s pattern of de-escalation headlines failing to drive a lasting sell-off. For traders, the main risks to the range are a surprise diplomatic breakthrough, which CITIC sees as unlikely, or an escalation that Congress and US public opinion fail to restrain.

---

From Beijing’s vantage point, the Iran war has settled into a stalemate that neither escalates nor ends, with the US blockade as its defining feature.

Summary:

  • CITIC Securities says Republican midterm losses do not necessarily change the course of the US-Iran conflict
  • It expects the Trump administration to maintain a high-pressure economic blockade, keeping war risk “bounded”
  • Escalation is restrained by Congress’s control of war funding, US public opposition to a long war, and Israel’s reliance on US backing
  • De-escalation is blocked because Iran’s demands are unacceptable to both US parties and Washington lacks an exit strategy
  • The view matches recent signals: Trump favours keeping the blockade, while Tehran demands it be lifted first

The view from China: Republican losses in the US midterm elections do not necessarily change the trajectory of the US-Iran conflict, according to CITIC Securities. The brokerage expects the Trump administration to keep up a high-pressure economic blockade on Tehran and the war to stay contained within clear limits.

The Chinese brokerage describes Middle East war risk as being in a bounded state. In its view, the risk of escalation is controllable, while a negotiated de-escalation remains blocked. It argues that Iran’s strategic aims leave no room for compromise with either of the main US parties.

CITIC sees several brakes on escalation. Congress holds leverage over war funding, and US public opposition to a prolonged conflict with Iran reduces the political payoff from widening it. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also has limited scope to expand operations without US backing.

At the same time, the brokerage sees little prospect of a negotiated exit. It says Iran’s strategic demands are unacceptable to Democrats and Republicans alike, and Washington lacks a feasible exit strategy. That leaves the conflict stuck between the two extremes.

The assessment matches the latest signals from both sides. US President Donald Trump said this week that renewed military action looks unlikely and that Gulf states prefer to keep the naval blockade in place. Meanwhile, Iran’s top security official told Washington to accept Tehran’s seven conditions, including an end to the blockade, before any talks.

For oil, a bounded conflict cuts both ways. A lower risk of escalation limits the scope for a renewed spike in prices. But a blockade with no exit keeps Iranian supply constrained and the Strait of Hormuz disrupted, leaving a floor under crude.

---

CITIC Securities is one of China’s largest securities firms and is widely described as its biggest brokerage. Founded in 1995, it offers investment banking, brokerage, research and asset management, and is listed in Shanghai and Hong Kong. It is part of the state-owned CITIC Group conglomerate and owns the regional broker CLSA, which runs much of its international business.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UK retail sales rise 1.5%, best since June, but fuel costs and Budget caution weigh
item.description:
The data give a mixed signal for UK rates and sterling. Headline spending is firmer, but much of the gain reflects higher fuel prices, so it shows energy costs rather than stronger real demand. That supports the view that the oil shock is acting as a tax on households, which tends to weigh on discretionary spending and confidence over time. Flat non-food sales and the weakest confidence since April argue against reading the numbers as a pickup in underlying consumer momentum. Any easing in oil prices from Middle East de-escalation would offer households relief at the pump, while the Budget remains a near-term source of caution for spending and for the pound.

-

Earlier:

  • Markets price three more BoE hikes, but analysts see a shallower path after move to 4%

-

Britons spent more in October, but mostly on fuel and food, and they feel gloomier about the economy than at any point since April.

Summary:

  • BRC total retail sales rose 1.5% year on year in October, from 1.3% in September and the strongest since June; like-for-like sales rose 1.1%
  • Food sales rose 3.2% while non-food sales were flat, with some shoppers waiting for Black Friday deals
  • Higher household costs and caution ahead of the Budget kept growth modest
  • Barclays card spending rose 2.3%, the biggest increase since July 2025, with essential spending up 3.1% on a 22.7% jump in fuel spending
  • Barclays’ consumer confidence gauge fell to its weakest since April

UK retail sales grew modestly in October, the British Retail Consortium said on Tuesday. Higher petrol prices, caution ahead of the Budget and shoppers holding off for Black Friday deals kept a lid on spending, even as a separate card-spending survey from Barclays showed the strongest growth in more than a year.

Total retail sales rose 1.5% from a year earlier, up from 1.3% in September and the strongest increase since June, according to the BRC. Like-for-like sales, which strip out changes in store space, rose 1.1% after 1.0% the previous month. Food sales climbed 3.2% while non-food sales were flat, a split that points to price-driven grocery spending rather than a broad pickup in discretionary demand. The BRC noted that sales of cupboard staples rose modestly after the government advised households to stock up for emergencies.

Commentary accompanying the survey described overall growth as modest, citing higher household costs, caution ahead of the Budget and consumers waiting for Black Friday discounts.

Barclays’ data, which covers card spending on a wider range of goods and services, painted a firmer picture. Consumer spending rose 2.3% year on year in October, up from 2.0% in September and the biggest increase since July 2025. Essential spending grew 3.1%, driven by a 22.7% jump in spending on fuel, while non-essential spending rose 1.9%. Entertainment had its strongest month since September 2024 as tickets for the Glastonbury music festival went on sale.

The fuel figure shows how higher energy costs are inflating headline spending. Much of the increase reflects households paying more at the pump rather than buying more, which squeezes budgets for other goods.

That strain shows up in sentiment. Barclays said consumer confidence in the UK economy was at its weakest since April, suggesting households remain wary despite the steadier spending figures. Non-food sales were flat, and Black Friday is likely to pull some purchases into late November. That leaves October’s numbers as a mixed read on UK consumer demand heading into the key holiday trading period. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia business conditions hit six-year low as forward orders slide: NAB
item.description:
The survey strengthens the case that the RBA’s five hikes this year are biting, and lowers the odds of a sixth. Elevated input costs and underlying inflation well above target still argue against any early pivot to easing. That leaves the cash rate on hold at 4.85%, a stance that offers the Australian dollar little support from rate expectations. Softer domestic data compound the pressure on the Aussie, which is already trading as a proxy for AI-linked equity sentiment. Australian bond yields at the front end are the most likely to respond if markets start pricing cuts further out.

--

Australian firms are being squeezed from both sides, with demand fading and costs still climbing, which is exactly the bind the RBA now faces.

Summary:

  • NAB’s business conditions index fell 1 point to -2 in October, the lowest since August 2020, as forward orders dropped sharply
  • Business confidence fell 1 point to -15, far below its long-run average of +5
  • Retail reported the weakest confidence, conditions and forward orders, and construction also softened
  • Purchase cost growth rose 0.1 percentage point to a quarterly 2.4%
  • NAB says cost pressures remain a risk to inflation while slowing growth threatens labour demand
  • The RBA has hiked five times this year to 4.85%, an 18-year high; underlying inflation was 3.6% in September

Australian business conditions fell to their weakest level in six years in October as forward orders dropped sharply, a National Australia Bank survey showed on Tuesday. The survey points to slowing domestic demand under the weight of higher borrowing costs and persistent cost pressures.

The survey’s business conditions index slipped 1 point to -2, the lowest reading since August 2020. Business confidence also fell 1 point, to -15, far below its long-run average of +5. NAB said conditions have been trending gradually lower in recent months, suggesting growth has slowed further in the second half of 2026 from an already softer first half.

Retail reported the weakest confidence, conditions and forward orders of any industry. Construction, which had held up well this year, also showed signs of softening.

Costs remain a sticking point. Purchase cost growth picked up 0.1 percentage point to a quarterly rate of 2.4%, keeping input price pressures elevated even as demand slows.

That combination sums up the Reserve Bank of Australia’s dilemma, according to NAB. The bank said cost pressures remain a serious risk to the inflation outlook, but growth is slowing and labour demand may soften in the months ahead. The RBA has raised rates five times this year, taking the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85%, in response to stubborn inflation. Underlying inflation was running at an annual 3.6% in September, well above the central bank’s 2% to 3% target band.

The survey adds to signs that the RBA’s tightening is biting. With forward orders falling and confidence deeply negative, the case for further hikes looks weaker, though elevated costs and above-target inflation make an early shift toward easing unlikely. For the Australian dollar, already under pressure from the slide in AI-linked stocks, softer domestic data add another reason for caution. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
